text: Barry Morris Goldwater (January 2, 1909 – May 29, 1998) was an American politician and major general in the Air Force Reserve who served as a United States senator from 1953 to 1965 and 1969 to 1987, and was the Republican Party's nominee for president in 1964. Born in Phoenix, Arizona, in what was then the Arizona Territory, he was the son of Baron M. Goldwater and Hattie Josephine "JoJo" Williams; his father's family founded Goldwater's Department Store, a leading upscale department store in Phoenix. Goldwater's paternal grandfather, Michel Goldwasser, a Polish Jew born in 1821 in Konin, then part of Congress Poland, emigrated to London after the Revolutions of 1848, anglicized his name to Michael Goldwater, and married Sarah Nathan, a member of an English-Jewish family, in the Great Synagogue of London. The Goldwaters later emigrated to the United States, first arriving in San Francisco, California, before settling in the Arizona Territory, where Michael Goldwater opened a small department store that was later expanded by his sons Henry, Baron, and Morris. Morris Goldwater (1852–1939) was an Arizona territorial and state legislator, mayor of Prescott, Arizona, delegate to the Arizona Constitutional Convention, and later President of the Arizona State Senate. Goldwater was raised in his mother's Episcopal faith, though he identified as Episcopalian throughout his life and occasionally referred to himself as Jewish. After performing poorly academically as a high school freshman, he attended Staunton Military Academy in Virginia, where he played varsity football, basketball, track, and swimming, served as senior class treasurer, and attained the rank of captain. He graduated in 1928 and enrolled at the University of Arizona but dropped out after one year. Barry Goldwater is the most recent non-college graduate to be the nominee of a major political party in a presidential election. He entered the family business around the time of his father's death in 1930 and took over the department store six years later, though he was not particularly enthusiastic about running it. During World War II, Goldwater received a reserve commission in the U.S. Army Air Force, trained as a pilot, and was assigned to the Ferry Command, flying aircraft and supplies between the U.S. and India via the Azores, North Africa, South America, Nigeria, and Central Africa, including "The Hump," a dangerous route over the Himalayas to deliver supplies to the Republic of China. After the war, he was a leading proponent of creating the United States Air Force Academy and served on its Board of Visitors; the visitor center at the academy is now named in his honor. He remained in the Army Air Reserve, founded the Arizona Air National Guard in 1946 at the rank of Colonel, ordered it to be desegregated two years before the rest of the U.S. military, and in the early 1960s commanded the 9999th Air Reserve Squadron as a major general. He was instrumental in pushing the Pentagon to support the desegregation of the armed services and retired from the Arizona Air National Guard in 1967 as a major general. As a U.S. Senator, Goldwater was known for his direct style and became a conservative Republican and friend of Herbert Hoover. He was outspoken against New Deal liberalism, especially its ties to labor unions, and criticized President Dwight Eisenhower's policies as too liberal, including opposing his $71.8 billion budget and his nomination of Earl Warren for Chief Justice. He supported the integration of the Senate cafeteria after insisting that his Black legislative assistant, Katherine Maxwell, be served alongside all other employees. Goldwater supported racial equality by integrating his family's business in the 1930s, helping found the NAACP's Arizona chapter, ensuring the Arizona Air National Guard was racially integrated from its inception in 1946, and working with Phoenix civil rights leaders to integrate public schools a year before Brown v. Board of Education. He supported the Civil Rights Acts of 1957 and 1960 and the 24th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution but opposed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, disagreeing with Titles II and VII, which dealt with employment, and later called his vote against it "one of his greatest regrets." In his 1960 book The Conscience of a Conservative, he stated that he supported the objectives of Brown v. Board of Education but argued that the federal government had no role in ordering states to desegregate schools, believing that social and cultural change should be handled by the people directly involved. He voted in favor of the Civil Rights Act of 1957 and the 24th Amendment, did not vote on the 1960 Act due to absence when the vote was announced, and voted against the 1964 Act on the floor despite having supported it in committee. He was absent during President John F. Kennedy's nomination of Byron White to the Supreme Court in 1962 but was present when Arthur Goldberg was confirmed. Goldwater became the frontrunner for the GOP presidential nomination after the success of The Conscience of a Conservative, despite being viewed as too far right by moderate and liberal Republicans, who recruited opponents such as Nelson Rockefeller, Henry Cabot Lodge Jr., and William Scranton. He won a multi-candidate race for the nomination with strong support from Southern Republicans, including 271 of 279 Southern convention delegates. Eisenhower supported Goldwater, stating he was not an extremist and that they were all Republicans. Liberal Republicans opposed his candidacy, fearing his militant anti-communism would lead to nuclear war; prominent Republicans including Kenneth B. Keating, Jacob Javits, William Scranton, George Romney, and John V. Lindsay refused to endorse him. Jackie Robinson walked out of the convention in protest. Goldwater delivered a well-received acceptance speech, which he prepared more carefully than any other speech in his career. In the 1964 U.S. presidential election, Goldwater mobilized a large conservative constituency to win the Republican nomination but lost the general election to incumbent Democratic president Lyndon B. Johnson in a landslide. After leaving the Senate, Goldwater returned in 1969 and specialized in defense and foreign policy. Along with Jay Rhodes and Hugh Scott, he successfully urged President Richard Nixon to resign in 1974 when evidence of a cover-up in the Watergate scandal became overwhelming and impeachment was imminent. In 1986, he oversaw passage of the Goldwater–Nichols Act, which strengthened civilian authority in the U.S. Department of Defense. Near the end of his career, Goldwater's views on social and cultural issues grew increasingly libertarian. Many political pundits and historians believe he laid the foundation for the conservative revolution that followed, helping to bring about the presidency of Ronald Reagan in the 1980s and having a substantial impact on the American libertarian movement. After leaving office, Goldwater became supportive of environmental protection, gay rights including military service and adoption rights for same-sex couples, abortion rights, and the legalization of marijuana. He was an early member and largely unrecognized supporter of the National Urban League's Phoenix chapter, covering its early operating deficits with personal funds, and was later honored with the 1991 Humanitarian Award for 50 years of loyal service to the Phoenix Urban League. Despite being denounced by the NAACP during his presidential run, the Urban League recognized his contributions. Goldwater defeated veteran Democrat and Senate Majority Leader Ernest McFarland in the 1952 Arizona Senate election by 12,600 votes in Maricopa County, almost double the overall margin of 6,725 votes, and won again in 1958, becoming the first Arizona Republican to win a second term in the U.S. Senate. During his Senate career, he was regarded as the "Grand Old Man of the Republican Party and one of the nation's most respected exponents of conservatism." He was also known for a sign in his office: "There are old pilots and there are bold pilots, but there are no old, bold pilots."

The demand for active measures to defeat the Soviet Union was feared to foment a nuclear war. Besides Rockefeller, prominent Republican office-holders refused to endorse Goldwater's candidacy, including Republican senators from New York Kenneth B. Keating and Jacob Javits, Pennsylvania governor William Scranton, Michigan governor George Romney, and Congressman John V. Lindsay (NY-17). Rockefeller Republican Jackie Robinson walked out of the convention in disgust over Goldwater's nomination. Henry Cabot Lodge Jr., Richard Nixon's running mate in 1960, opposed Goldwater, calling his proposal to realign the Democrat and Republican parties into two Liberal and Conservative parties "totally abhorrent" and stating that no one in their right mind should oppose the federal government in having a role in the future of America. In the face of such opposition, Goldwater delivered a well-received acceptance speech, which he devoted more care to than to any other speech in his political career, as he would deliver it to the largest and most attentive audience of his life. According to author Lee Edwards, the speech reflected his conservative views boldly but not irrationally, and Goldwater challenged critics of extremism head-on. In his own words: "Extremism in the defense of liberty is no vice!" and "Moderation in the pursuit of justice is no virtue!" This paraphrase of Cicero was suggested by Harry V. Jaffa, though the speech was primarily written by Karl Hess. Because President Johnson was popular, Goldwater refrained from attacking him directly and did not mention Johnson by name in his convention speech. Although raised as an Episcopalian, Goldwater was the first candidate of Jewish descent, through his father, to be nominated for president by a major American party. After securing the Republican nomination, Goldwater chose RNC Chairman William E. Miller as his running mate, joking that he chose Miller because "he drives Johnson nuts." Miller was ideologically aligned with Goldwater's conservative wing and balanced the ticket as a practicing Catholic from the East Coast, though he had low name recognition and was viewed as a skilled political strategist. Former U.S. senator Prescott Bush, a moderate Republican from Connecticut, was a friend of Goldwater and supported him in the general election. Future chief justice William H. Rehnquist first gained national Republican attention through his work as a legal adviser to Goldwater's campaign, having begun his law practice in 1953 in the firm of Denison Kitchel of Phoenix, Goldwater's national campaign manager and friend of nearly three decades. Goldwater's advocacy of active interventionism to prevent the spread of communism and defend American values and allies led to counterattacks from Lyndon B. Johnson and his supporters, who claimed that Goldwater's militancy would have dire consequences, possibly even nuclear war. In a May 1964 speech, Goldwater suggested nuclear weapons should be treated like conventional weapons and used in Vietnam, specifically that they should have been used at Dien Bien Phu in 1954 to defoliate trees. Regarding Vietnam, Goldwater charged that Johnson's policy lacked "goal, course, or purpose," leaving "only sudden death in the jungles and the slow strangulation of freedom." Goldwater's rhetoric on nuclear war was viewed as uncompromising, supported by comments such as, "Let's lob one into the men's room at the Kremlin," and he advocated that field commanders in Vietnam and Europe should be given the authority to use tactical nuclear weapons (which he called "small conventional nuclear weapons") without presidential confirmation. Goldwater countered Johnson's attacks by criticizing the administration for ethical lapses and stating in a commercial that "we, as a nation, are not far from the kind of moral decay that has brought on the fall of other nations and people.... I say it is time to put conscience back in government. And by good example, put it back in all walks of American life." Goldwater campaign commercials included statements of support by actor Raymond Massey and moderate Republican senator Margaret Chase Smith. Before the 1964 election, Fact magazine, published by Ralph Ginzburg, ran a special issue titled "The Unconscious of a Conservative: A Special Issue on the Mind of Barry Goldwater," which argued Goldwater was mentally unfit to be president, supported by a poll of 2,417 board-certified psychiatrists out of 12,356 who were surveyed, with 1,189 saying Goldwater was mentally incapable of holding the office, and most others declining to diagnose him, saying he was not psychologically unfit but would be negligent. After the election, Goldwater sued the publisher, editor, and magazine for libel in Goldwater v. Ginzburg. The jury awarded Goldwater $1.00 in compensatory damages against all three defendants, but $25,000 against Ginzburg and $50,000 against Fact magazine, Inc. According to Warren Boroson, then-managing editor of Fact and later a financial columnist, the main biography of Goldwater in the magazine was written by David Bar-Illan, the Israeli pianist. A Democratic campaign advertisement known as Daisy showed a young girl counting daisy petals from one to ten, followed by a voiceover counting down from ten to one, with the child's face shown as a still photograph and then images of nuclear explosions and mushroom clouds, ending with a plea to vote for Johnson, implying that Goldwater (though not named) would provoke a nuclear war if elected. The ad, which featured only a few spoken words and relied on imagery, was one of the most provocative in American political campaign history and is credited as the birth of the modern style of "negative political ads" on television. The ad aired only once and was immediately pulled, but was shown many times by local television stations covering the controversy. Goldwater did not have ties to the Ku Klux Klan (KKK), but was publicly endorsed by members of the organization. Lyndon B. Johnson exploited this association during the election, but Goldwater barred the KKK from supporting him and denounced them. Throughout the campaign, Goldwater refused to appeal to racial tensions or backlash against civil rights. After the Harlem riot of 1964, Goldwater privately gathered news reporters on his campaign plane and said that if anyone attempted to sow racial violence on his political behalf, he would withdraw from the presidential race—even if it was the day before the election. Past comments came back to haunt Goldwater. He had once called the Eisenhower administration "a dime-store New Deal," and Eisenhower never fully forgave him. However, Eisenhower did film a television commercial with Goldwater. Eisenhower qualified his voting for Goldwater in November by remarking that he had voted not specifically for Goldwater, but for the Republican Party. In December 1961, Goldwater told a news conference that "sometimes I think this country would be better off if we could just saw off the Eastern Seaboard and let it float out to sea," a comment that was used in a Johnson television commercial. Remarks about making Social Security voluntary and statements in Tennessee about selling the Tennessee Valley Authority, a large local New Deal employer, also drew criticism. The Goldwater campaign spotlighted Ronald Reagan, who appeared in a campaign ad. In turn, Reagan gave a stirring, nationally televised speech, "A Time for Choosing," in support of Goldwater. Goldwater only won his home state of Arizona and five states in the Deep South: Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, and South Carolina. The Southern states, traditionally Democratic up to that time, voted Republican primarily as a statement of opposition to the Civil Rights Act, which had been signed into law by Johnson earlier that year. Despite Johnson's support for the Civil Rights Act, the bill received split support from Congressional Democrats due to southerner opposition, while Congressional Republicans overwhelmingly supported it, with Goldwater being joined by only five other Republican senators in voting against it. All of the states carried by Goldwater, except Arizona, had voted against Republican nominee Richard Nixon just four years earlier. In carrying Georgia by a margin of 54–45%, Goldwater became the first Republican nominee to win the state. Goldwater's poor showing pulled down many supporters. Of the 57 Republican Congressmen who endorsed Goldwater before the convention, 20 were defeated for reelection, along with many promising young Republicans. In contrast, Republican Congressman John Lindsay (NY-17), who refused to endorse Goldwater, was handily re-elected in a district where Democrats held a 10% overall advantage. On the other hand, the defeat of so many older politicians created openings for young conservatives to move up the ladder. While the loss of moderate Republicans was temporary—they were back by 1966—Goldwater also permanently pulled many conservative Southerners and whites out of the New Deal Coalition. According to Steve Kornacki of Salon, Goldwater broke through and won five Southern states—the best showing in the region for a GOP candidate since Reconstruction. In Mississippi—where Franklin D. Roosevelt had won nearly 100 percent of the vote 28 years earlier—Goldwater claimed 87 percent. It has frequently been argued that Goldwater's strong performance in Southern states previously regarded as Democratic strongholds foreshadowed a larger shift in electoral trends in the coming decades that would make the South a Republican bastion (an end to the "Solid South")—first in presidential politics and eventually at the congressional and state levels. Also, Goldwater's uncompromising promotion of freedom was the start of a continuing shift in American politics from liberalism to a conservative economic philosophy. Throughout the late 1970s, as the conservative wing under Ronald Reagan gained control of the Republican Party, Goldwater concentrated on his Senate duties, especially in military affairs. Goldwater purportedly did not like Richard Nixon on either a political or personal level, later calling the California Republican "the most dishonest individual I have ever met in my life." Accordingly, he played little part in Nixon's election or administration, but he helped force Nixon's resignation in 1974. On August 7, 1974, at the height of the Watergate scandal, Goldwater led a delegation, which also included House Republican Leader John Jacob Rhodes and Senate Republican Leader Hugh Scott, who met with Nixon at the White House and urged him to resign. At the time, Nixon's impeachment by the House of Representatives was imminent and Goldwater warned him that fewer than 10 Republican senators would vote against conviction. Despite being a difficult year for Republican candidates, the 1974 election saw Goldwater easily reelected over his Democratic opponent, Jonathan Marshall, the publisher of The Scottsdale Progress. With regard to the 1976 Republican ticket, Goldwater helped block Nelson Rockefeller's renomination as vice president. When Reagan challenged Gerald Ford for the presidential nomination in 1976, Goldwater endorsed the incumbent Ford, looking for consensus rather than conservative idealism. As one historian notes, "The Arizonan had lost much of his zest for battle." In 1979, when President Carter normalized relations with Communist China, Goldwater and some other Senators sued him in the Supreme Court, arguing that the President could not terminate the Sino-American Mutual Defense Treaty with the Republic of China (Taiwan) without the approval of Congress. The case, Goldwater v. Carter (444 U.S. 996), was dismissed by the court as a political question. On June 9, 1969, Goldwater was absent during President Nixon's nomination of Warren E. Burger as Chief Justice of the United States while Senate Minority Whip Hugh Scott announced that Goldwater would have voted in favor if present. Goldwater voted in favor of Nixon's failed Supreme Court nomination of Clement Haynsworth on November 21, 1969, and a few months later, voted in favor of Nixon's failed Supreme Court nomination of Harrold Carswell on April 8, 1970. The following month, Goldwater was absent when Nixon nominee Harry Blackmun was confirmed on May 12, 1970, while Senate Minority Whip Robert P. Griffin announced that Goldwater would have voted in favor if present. On December 6, 1971, Goldwater voted in favor of Nixon's nomination of Lewis F. Powell Jr., and on December 10, Goldwater voted in favor of Nixon's nomination of William Rehnquist as Associate Justice. On December 17, 1975, Goldwater voted in favor of President Gerald Ford's nomination of John Paul Stevens to the Supreme Court. With his fourth Senate term due to end in January 1981, Goldwater seriously considered retiring from the Senate in 1980 before deciding to run for one final term. It was a surprisingly tough campaign for re-election. Goldwater was viewed by some as out of touch and vulnerable for several reasons, chiefly because he had planned to retire in 1981 and had not visited many areas of Arizona outside of Phoenix and Tucson. Additionally, his Democratic challenger, Bill Schulz, proved to be a formidable opponent. A former Republican and a wealthy real estate developer, Schulz's campaign slogan was "Energy for the Eighties." Arizona's changing population also hurt Goldwater. The state's population had greatly increased, and a large portion of the electorate had not lived in the state at the time Goldwater was previously elected, meaning unlike most incumbents, many voters were less familiar with Goldwater's actual beliefs. Goldwater spent most of the campaign on the defensive. Although he was eventually declared the winning candidate in the general election by a very narrow margin, receiving 49.5% of the vote to Schulz's 48.4%, early returns on election night indicated that Schulz would win. The counting of votes continued through the night and into the next morning. At around daybreak, Goldwater learned that he had been reelected thanks to absentee ballots, which were among the last to be counted. Goldwater's close victory in 1980 came despite Reagan's 61% landslide over Jimmy Carter in Arizona. Despite Goldwater's struggles, in 1980, Republicans were able to pick up 12 senate seats, regaining control of the chamber for the first time since 1955, when Goldwater was in his first term. Goldwater was now in the most powerful position he had ever been in the Senate. In October 1983, Goldwater voted against the legislation establishing Martin Luther King Jr. Day as a federal holiday. On September 21, 1981, Goldwater voted in favor of Reagan's Supreme Court nomination of Sandra Day O'Connor. Goldwater was absent during the nominations of William Rehnquist as Chief Justice of the United States and Antonin Scalia as Associate Justice on September 17, 1986. After the new Senate convened in January 1981, Goldwater became chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee. In this role he clashed with the Reagan administration in April 1984 when he discovered that the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) had been mining the waters of Nicaragua since February, something he had first denied when the matter was raised. In a note to CIA director William Casey, Goldwater denounced what he called an "act of war," saying that "this is no way to run a railroad," and stated crossly that only Congress had the power to declare war and accused the CIA of illegally mining Nicaraguan waters without the permission of Congress. Goldwater concluded, "The President has asked us to back his foreign policy. Bill, how can we back his foreign policy when we don't know what the hell he is doing? Lebanon, yes, we all knew that he sent troops over there. But mine the harbors in Nicaragua? This is an act violating international law. It is an act of war. For the life of me, I don't see how we are going to explain it." Goldwater felt compelled to issue an apology on the floor of the Senate because the Senate Intelligence Committee had failed in its duties to oversee the CIA as he stated, saying, "I am forced to apologize for the members of my committee because I did not know the facts on this case. And I apologize to all the members of the Senate for the same reason." Goldwater subsequently voted for a Congressional resolution condemning the mining. In his 1980 Senate reelection campaign, Goldwater won support from religious conservatives but in his final term voted consistently to uphold legal abortion and in 1981 gave a speech on how he was angry about the bullying of American politicians by religious organizations and would "fight them every step of the way." He introduced the 1984 Cable Franchise Policy and Communications Act, which allowed local governments to require the transmission of public, educational, and government access (PEG) channels, barred cable operators from exercising editorial control over the content of programs carried on PEG channels, and absolved them from liability for their content. Goldwater apologized on the floor of the Senate for the Senate Intelligence Committee's failure to oversee the CIA, stating he did not know the facts and apologizing to all Senate members for the same reason. He later voted in favor of a Congressional resolution condemning the mining. During his 1980 Senate reelection campaign, he won support from religious conservatives but, in his final term, consistently upheld legal abortion and delivered a speech in 1981 expressing anger at religious organizations bullying American politicians, vowing to "fight them every step of the way." He introduced the 1984 Cable Franchise Policy and Communications Act, which allowed local governments to require transmission of public, educational, and government access (PEG) channels, barred cable operators from editorial control over PEG content, and absolved them of liability for that content. On May 12, 1986, Goldwater was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Reagan. In response to Jerry Falwell's opposition to Sandra Day O'Connor's Supreme Court nomination, Goldwater retorted, "Every good Christian ought to kick Falwell right in the ass," though according to John Dean, he actually suggested kicking Falwell in the "nuts," with the media altering the reference. Goldwater also criticized President Reagan, particularly after the Iran–Contra Affair became public in 1986, saying it was "the god-damned stupidest foreign policy blunder this country's ever made," though he still considered Reagan a good president. He later stated that the close 1980 election result convinced him not to run again and retired in 1987, serving as Chair of the Senate Intelligence and Armed Services Committees in his final term. Despite being known as a firebrand in the 1960s, he was regarded as a stabilizing influence in the Senate and one of the most respected members of either major party, remaining staunchly anti-communist and "hawkish" on military issues, yet supporting the Panama Canal Treaty ratification in the 1970s and being a key supporter of the Goldwater–Nichols Act, which reorganized the U.S. military's senior-command structure. He was associated with anti-union work and anti-communism, supported the conservative coalition, and his labor-related work led to major anti-labor reforms in 1957; a campaign by the AFL–CIO challenged his 1958 reelection bid. He voted against censuring Senator Joseph McCarthy in 1954, who made unfounded claims about communists in the State Department without accusing individuals, and emphasized his opposition to global communism in his 1960 book The Conscience of a Conservative, which became a key text in conservative circles. In 1964, Goldwater ran a campaign emphasizing states' rights, which attracted conservatives, and voted for the Civil Rights Act of 1957 and the 24th Amendment, but did not vote on the 1960 Civil Rights Act due to absence, with Senate Minority Whip Thomas Kuchel stating he would have supported it if present; he opposed the 1964 Civil Rights Act, arguing that its private employment provisions would lead to racial quotas and interfere with private business decisions, though he had quietly supported civil rights in segregated Phoenix in the 1950s without using his name. His vote on the 1964 Act alienated voters outside the South, where he won all Deep South states (South Carolina, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana) for the first time since Reconstruction, contributing to his landslide defeat. His campaign promoted strictly fiscally conservative policies, criticizing President Johnson's war on poverty and claiming that poverty stemmed from lack of education or ambition, and called for ending agricultural subsidies, privatizing Social Security, and privatizing the Tennessee Valley Authority. His voting records showed alignment with other Republicans in Congress. In 1971, he sought to end U.S. funding of the United Nations after China's admission, stating he believed it would cause the UN to collapse and move its headquarters to Peking or Moscow. Though less influential than Reagan after 1965, Goldwater shaped and redefined the conservative movement from the late 1950s to 1964. Arizona Senator John McCain, who succeeded him in 1987, said he transformed the Republican Party from an Eastern elitist organization into the breeding ground for Ronald Reagan's election. Columnist George Will noted that Reagan's 1980 victory was the culmination of 16 years of building support for Goldwater from the 1964 campaign. After the 1964 defeat, the Republican Party gained 47 House seats in 1966. In January 1969, Goldwater wrote in National Review that he was not against liberals, saw them as a counterweight to conservatism, and named Max Lerner as an example. He supported environmental protection, stating in 1965 that the Nixon administration was correct in cracking down on pollution and that government action was necessary to halt pollution at the source, even if it harmed the economy. By the 1980s, with Reagan as president and the religious right gaining influence, Goldwater's libertarian views on personal issues were revealed; he viewed abortion as a personal choice and supported abortion rights, seeing religious right views as an encroachment on personal liberty. Though he voted against making Martin Luther King's birthday a national holiday in his final term, he later expressed support. In 1987, he received the Langley Gold Medal from the Smithsonian Institution; in 1988, Princeton University's American Whig-Cliosophic Society awarded him the James Madison Award for Distinguished Public Service. After retiring in 1987, he described Arizona Governor Evan Mecham as "hardheaded" and urged him to resign, and two years later claimed the Republican party had been taken over by "a bunch of kooks." During the 1988 presidential campaign, he told vice-presidential nominee Dan Quayle at a campaign event in Arizona, "I want you to go back and tell George Bush to start talking about the issues." In the 1990s, some of his statements alienated social conservatives; he endorsed Democrat Karan English in an Arizona congressional race, urged Republicans to distance themselves from Bill Clinton over the Whitewater scandal, and criticized the military's ban on homosexuals, stating "Everyone knows that gays have served honorably in the military since at least the time of Julius Caesar" and "You don't need to be 'straight' to fight and die for your country. You just need to shoot straight," and warned establishment Republicans not to associate his name with their actions, calling them extremists who had harmed the Republican party more than Democrats. In a 1994 interview with The Washington Post, he said that when people refer to "radical right," they often mean moneymaking ventures by figures like Pat Robertson attempting to turn the Republican Party into a religious organization, warning that such a shift would end politics. In November 1994, he reiterated his concerns about religious groups gaining control of the Republican Party, stating that Republicans were "selling their soul" to win elections and that such preachers, who believe they act in God's name, cannot or will not compromise, which he saw as a threat to governance. In 1996, he told Bob Dole, whose campaign received weak support from conservative Republicans, "We're the new liberals of the Republican party. Can you imagine that?" That same year, with Senator Dennis DeConcini, he endorsed an Arizona initiative to legalize medical marijuana despite opposition from social conservatives. In 1934, Goldwater married Margaret "Peggy" Johnson, daughter of a prominent Indiana industrialist; they had four children: Joanne (born January 18, 1936), Barry Jr. (born July 15, 1938), Michael (born March 15, 1940), and Peggy (born July 27, 1944). He became a widower in 1985 and married Susan Wechsler, a nurse 32 years his junior, in 1992. His son Barry Goldwater Jr. served as a Republican Congressman representing California from 1969 to 1983. His grandson Ty Ross, an interior designer and former Zoli model who is openly gay and HIV positive, has been credited with inspiring Goldwater to become an octogenarian proponent of gay civil rights. Goldwater ran track and cross country in high school, specializing in the 880 yard run. In 1940, he became one of the first to run the Colorado River recreationally through the Grand Canyon, rowing as an oarsman on Norman Nevills' second commercial trip from Green River, Utah, to Lake Mead. In 1970, the Arizona Historical Foundation published his daily journal from the journey, including photographs, in a 209-page volume titled Delightful Journey. In 1963, he joined the Arizona Society of the Sons of the American Revolution; he was also a lifetime member of the Veterans of Foreign Wars, American Legion, and Sigma Chi fraternity, and belonged to both the York Rite and Scottish Rite of Freemasonry, receiving the 33rd degree in the Scottish Rite. He was an avid amateur radio operator from the early 1920s, using call signs 6BPI, K3UIG, and K7UGA, with the last used by an Arizona club honoring him. During the Vietnam War, he served as a Military Affiliate Radio System (MARS) operator. He was a spokesman for amateur radio, appearing in numerous educational and promotional films and videos from 1969 onward, produced by organizations such as Dave Bell (W6AQ), John R. Griggs (W6KW), Alan Kaul (W6RCL), Forrest Oden (N6ENV), and Roy Neal (K6DUE), with his first appearance in Dave Bell's The World of Amateur Radio and his last on-screen ham radio appearance in 1994 explaining an upcoming Earth-orbiting relay satellite. Electronics was another hobby, with Goldwater assembling more than 100 Heathkits and visiting their maker in Benton Harbor, Michigan, before the company ended the kit business in 1992. In 1916, he visited the Hopi reservation with architect John Rinker Kibby and obtained his first kachina doll; his collection eventually totaled 437 dolls, presented to the Heard Museum in Phoenix in 1969. He was an amateur photographer, leaving about 15,000 images to three Arizona institutions; he used a 4×5 Graflex, Rolleiflex, 16 mm Bell and Howell motion picture camera, and 35 mm Nikkormat FT, and was a member of the Royal Photographic Society from 1941, becoming a Life Member in 1948. For decades, he contributed photographs of Arizona to Arizona Highways, recognized for his Western landscapes and images of Native Americans; three books with his photographs are People and Places (1967), Barry Goldwater and the Southwest (1976), and Delightful Journey (1940, reprinted 1970), with Ansel Adams writing a foreword to the 1976 book. His photography occasionally intersected with politics; when President Kennedy invited former colleagues to the White House, Goldwater brought his camera and photographed Kennedy, who returned the photo with the inscription: "For Barry Goldwater—Whom I urge to follow the career for which he has shown such talent—photography!—from his friend—John Kennedy," a quip that became a classic of American political humor and was later relayed by Bennett Cerf; the photo was prized by Goldwater and sold for $17,925 in a 2010 Heritage auction. Son Michael Prescott Goldwater formed the Goldwater Family Foundation to make his father's photography available online, launching Barry Goldwater Photographs in September 2006 to coincide with the HBO documentary Mr. Conservative, produced by granddaughter CC Goldwater. On March 28, 1975, Goldwater wrote to Shlomo Arnon that he had long been interested in UFOs, having attempted to access classified information at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base about 10 to 12 years earlier and being denied the request, noting it remained classified above Top Secret; he expressed that he was just as eager as Arnon to see the material and hoped it would be released.

The quip "I'm liberal to a degree, I want everybody to be free. But if you think I'll let Barry Goldwater move in next door and marry my daughter, you must think I'm crazy" from Bob Dylan's song "I Shall Be Free No. 10" became a classic of American political humor after being relayed by humorist Bennett Cerf. Barry Goldwater prized a photo of himself with his friend John Kennedy, which he kept for the rest of his life and sold for $17,925 in a 2010 Heritage auction. His son, Michael Prescott Goldwater, formed the Goldwater Family Foundation to make his father's photography available online, launching the website Barry Goldwater Photographs in September 2006 to coincide with the HBO documentary Mr. Conservative: Goldwater on Goldwater, co-produced by granddaughter CC Goldwater and longtime friend Tani L. Cohen. On March 28, 1975, Goldwater wrote to Shlomo Arnon that he had long been interested in UFOs and, about ten or twelve years prior, had attempted to access information stored at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, which was denied and remains classified above Top Secret. He expressed hope that the evidence would be released soon, stating he was "just as anxious to see this material as you are." This effort was recounted in an April 25, 1988, interview with The New Yorker and again in a 1994 Larry King Live interview, where he said he believed the government knew about the material and that when he asked General Curtis LeMay if he could visit the secret room at Wright-Patterson, LeMay reacted angrily, cursing him and telling him never to ask again. Goldwater's public appearances ended in late 1996 after a massive stroke, and family members revealed he was in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease. He died on May 29, 1998, at age 89, in Paradise Valley, Arizona, from complications of the stroke. His funeral was conducted by both a Christian minister and a rabbi, and his ashes were buried at Episcopal Christ Church of the Ascension in Paradise Valley. A memorial statue was erected in a small park in Paradise Valley near his home and resting place. Buildings and monuments named after Barry Goldwater include the Barry M. Goldwater Terminal at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport, Goldwater Memorial Park in Paradise Valley, Arizona, the Barry Goldwater Air Force Academy Visitor Center at the United States Air Force Academy, and Barry Goldwater High School in northern Phoenix. In 2010, former Arizona Attorney General Grant Woods, a Goldwater scholar and supporter, founded the Goldwater Women's Tennis Classic Tournament at the Phoenix Country Club. On February 11, 2015, a statue of Goldwater by Deborah Copenhaver Fellows was unveiled by U.S. House and Senate leaders in National Statuary Hall of the U.S. Capitol. Barry Goldwater Peak is the highest peak in the White Tank Mountains. On December 9, 2016, Phoenix Sky Harbor Air National Guard Base was renamed Goldwater Air National Guard Base. The Barry M. Goldwater Scholarship and Excellence in Education Program was established by Congress in 1986 to provide scholarships to college students pursuing careers in science, mathematics, and engineering, awarding about 400 students (college sophomores and juniors) $7,500 per academic year (for their senior year or junior and senior years), honoring Goldwater's interest in science and technology. Goldwater's nephew Don Goldwater sought the Republican nomination for governor of Arizona in 2006 but was defeated by Len Munsil. His son Barry Goldwater Jr. served as a Congressman from California from 1969 to 1983, becoming the first Congressman to serve while his father was in the Senate. Goldwater's uncle Morris Goldwater served in the Arizona territorial and state legislatures and as mayor of Prescott, Arizona.
